opus-5.5.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you mean by "upper bound." There are obviously physical limits on computation. You've got a finite amount of matter and energy you can access, there are thermodynamic limits on how much computation you can do per unit of energy, there's the speed of light limiting how fast different parts of a system can communicate. So in that sense, sure, there's some ceiling on how much cognitive work can get done in a given region of space over a given amount of time.

But I don't think that's usually what people are asking. Usually the question is something like: is human-level intelligence close to the ceiling, such that AI systems might be somewhat smarter than us but not dramatically so? And there I'm pretty skeptical. When I look at the human brain, it seems like it was shaped by a lot of constraints that have nothing to do with the fundamental limits of cognition. It has to fit through a birth canal, it runs on about twenty watts, neurons fire at maybe a couple hundred hertz, and evolution only had a limited amount of time to optimize it for a world that looks very different from the one we live in now. Those all seem like pretty contingent constraints, and machines don't share most of them.

The other way I think about it is in terms of tasks. For a lot of specific domains, like chess or Go or protein structure prediction, we've already seen systems go well past the best humans, and it doesn't look like humans were sitting near some natural plateau. In some domains you might eventually hit diminishing returns. If a problem is just fundamentally hard, or the world is chaotic enough that more thinking doesn't buy you much better predictions, then extra intelligence helps less. Forecasting the weather a month out might be like that. But in a lot of the domains that matter most, like doing science, designing technology, or coordinating large projects, it seems like there's a lot of headroom.

So my overall view is that yes, there are ultimately physical limits, but I'd expect them to sit far above where humans are, and the more practically relevant question is how fast we approach them and what happens along the way.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different senses of that question, and they come apart pretty quickly.

One sense is: is there some ceiling on cognitive capability in principle, like a point where no possible system could be smarter? And I'm pretty skeptical that there's a meaningful ceiling there, in the sense that matters. There are physical limits, obviously. You can only do so much computation per unit of energy, you have light-speed delays, that kind of thing. But those limits are so far above where humans are that they're basically irrelevant for the questions people actually care about.

The sense that I think is actually interesting is more like: how much does being smarter keep buying you? Because "intelligence" isn't a single scalar that you crank up and everything gets better. It's a bunch of capabilities, and for each task there's some point of diminishing returns. If you're playing tic-tac-toe, there's a very low ceiling. You play optimally and then there's nothing more to do. For chess, the ceiling is higher but you still eventually saturate. For something like "predict what the weather will be in three weeks," there's a hard limit coming from chaos, and no amount of intelligence gets you past it. So for a lot of tasks, the right picture isn't "intelligence is unbounded," it's "the task has a bound, and sufficiently capable systems hit it."

Then the question is, what fraction of the things we care about look like tic-tac-toe versus things where returns keep going? And I think there are a lot of domains, especially things like designing technology, doing science, running organizations, where humans are clearly nowhere near the limit. Like, you look at how humans do engineering and it's obviously bottlenecked on us being slow and forgetful and bad at holding lots of things in our heads at once. So I expect a lot of headroom there, maybe a very large amount.

The other thing I'd say is that even when you're pretty close to the ceiling on quality, you're usually not close to the ceiling on speed or on scale. A system that thinks as well as the best human but a thousand times faster, or that runs a million copies in parallel that can coordinate well, is a very different thing from a human even if no individual thought it has is better than the best human thought. So people sometimes argue about whether there's an upper bound on intelligence as if that settles how big the impact of AI is, and I don't think it does. You can get a really transformative outcome just from speed and quantity, without needing to posit some qualitatively superhuman kind of cognition.

So my overall view is something like: there probably isn't a ceiling that matters, but also the question is kind of less important than it sounds. Most of the action is in how fast returns diminish on the specific tasks that drive economic and technological change, and I think for those the returns are large enough that we should expect things to look pretty wild well before we're bumping up against anything like a fundamental limit.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you’re holding fixed. If you fix the amount of computation, the data you can observe, and the time you have to act, then there’s some limit to how well you can do. You can’t predict a coin flip if you don’t have information about how the coin was flipped, and you can’t solve an arbitrarily hard computational problem with a fixed amount of computation.

But that’s quite different from asking whether there’s some level of intelligence beyond which getting smarter stops being useful. I don’t see a strong reason to expect that ceiling to be close to humans. We can already describe problems where you could spend vastly more computation and keep getting better answers.

There’s also a distinction between having better ideas and having more capacity to apply them. Maybe you eventually discover something like the best algorithms for thinking, but you can still run those algorithms for longer, or run more copies in parallel, or build a larger civilization that acquires more information.

So I’m more interested in the shape of the returns than in whether there’s an ultimate upper bound. How much better can you do with ten times as much computation? How much does that improvement help you build the next generation of computers? Those questions seem much more relevant to what happens with AI than whether intelligence is literally unbounded.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are physical limits on how much computation you can do, and that puts some upper bound on intelligence. But that’s a different question from whether there’s a level beyond which being smarter stops helping you very much.

For a particular problem, you can hit diminishing returns pretty quickly. If I ask you to play tic-tac-toe, there’s only so good you can get. If I ask you to predict something where the information just isn’t available, thinking harder won’t necessarily help. But across the whole range of things we care about—doing science, designing technology, figuring out how to organize people—I don’t see a strong reason to think humans are close to that point.

There’s also this distinction between having better algorithms and having more resources. Even if you’d found the best possible way to think, you could still accomplish more by running more copies, thinking for longer, or gathering more evidence. So I’m skeptical of treating intelligence as a single number with a clear ceiling. The question I care more about is how much room there is above humans for systems to do consequential things better than we can. And my guess is that there’s a lot.
